title: Rank-one subgroups and normalizer reflections
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness, connectedness and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-morphism-conventions]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. A smooth group is unipotent if every geometric point is a unipotent matrix in a faithful linear representation, meaning $(u-I)^n=0$ for some $n\geq1$. A reductive group is smooth and connected and has no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. A torus is a group isomorphic over $F$ to $\mathbf G_m^r$, where $r\geq0$ and $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ for a commutative $F$-algebra $A$; a maximal torus is a torus subgroup maximal under inclusion. Let $G$ be reductive and $T\subseteq G$ a maximal torus. Put $X=\operatorname{Hom}(T,\mathbf G_m)$ and $Y=\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf G_m,T)$, paired by $\chi\circ\nu(t)=t^{\langle\chi,\nu\rangle}$. For the adjoint action on the tangent space $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)$ one has a finite weight decomposition $\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha$, with $\Phi\subset X\setminus\{0\}$. The group $W=N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$ is finite and acts on $X,Y$, preserving the pairing and permuting $\Phi$; $N_G(T)$ denotes the subgroup functor normalizing $T$ after every scalar extension. For each $\alpha\in\Phi$, let $T_\alpha$ be the largest subtorus of $\ker\alpha$ and let $G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)$ be its centralizer: its $A$-points commute with every point of $T_\alpha$ after every commutative $A$-algebra extension. The group $G_\alpha$ is reductive of semisimple rank one, meaning that its quotient by its largest smooth connected normal solvable subgroup has maximal tori of dimension one. Write $\operatorname{SL}_2(A)$ for the $2\times2$ matrices over $A$ of determinant one. There is $v_\alpha:\operatorname{SL}_2\to G_\alpha$, with central kernel and image the derived subgroup, whose restriction to the upper unitriangular subgroup identifies it with a one-dimensional root subgroup of Lie algebra $\mathfrak g_\alpha$. Set $\alpha^\vee(t)=v_\alpha(\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1}))\in Y$. There is a unique nonidentity element of $N_{G_\alpha}(T)(F)/T(F)$; its image $s_\alpha\in W$ acts by $s_\alpha(x)=x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$ and $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$. The cocharacter satisfying this reflection identity is unique, and conjugation by $n\in N_G(T)(F)$ carries $\alpha^\vee$ to $(n\alpha)^\vee$. One has $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=1$ and $\mathbf Q\alpha\cap\Phi=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$. These assertions hold in every characteristic; weights are torus characters, not their differentials.

source.place: Propositions 21.1--21.2 and weight decomposition, pp.424--425; Theorem 21.11(a)--(e) and its rank-one SL2 construction, pp.428--430; equivariance is uniqueness in 21.11(e) after conjugating the rank-one subgroup.

proof.text: Choose $T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$. Character antiduality identifies $X=\mathbf Z^r$ and $Y=\operatorname{Hom}(X,\mathbf Z)$ with the stated perfect pairing. Apply the multiplicative-group weight decomposition successively to the $r$ commuting coordinate actions on $\mathfrak g$; each coordinate preserves the preceding weight spaces. This gives a finite decomposition by torus characters. The zero-weight space equals $\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(T))$: a tangent vector is an element over $F[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ reducing to the identity, and membership in the centralizer says precisely that its conjugate by every $t$, after every algebra extension, is itself. The self-centralizer theorem gives $C_G(T)=T$, hence the zero-weight space is $\operatorname{Lie}(T)$.

source.place: Chapter 21(a), printed pp.424--425; Proposition 10.34, printed pp.197--198.

proof.text: The normalizer-component lemma and $C_G(T)=T$ make $W=N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$ finite. For $n\in N_G(T)(F)$ define $(n\chi)(t)=\chi(n^{-1}tn)$ and $(n\nu)(z)=n\nu(z)n^{-1}$. Composing these maps shows that the integer pairing is preserved, and elements of $T(F)$ act trivially. If $v\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$, then $t\operatorname{Ad}(n)v=\operatorname{Ad}(n)(n^{-1}tn)v=\alpha(n^{-1}tn)\operatorname{Ad}(n)v$, so $\operatorname{Ad}(n)$ identifies $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ with $\mathfrak g_{n\alpha}$. This proves the root-permutation assertion.

Fix a root $\alpha\ne0$. Character antiduality and the largest-subtorus lemma identify $S=T_\alpha$ as follows: write $\alpha=m a$ with $a$ primitive in the free lattice $X$, and complete $a$ to an integral basis. In the corresponding torus coordinates $S$ is the subtorus with first coordinate $1$, of codimension one. A character is trivial on $S$ exactly when it belongs to $\mathbf Z a=X\cap\mathbf Q\alpha$. The dual-number argument in step 1, now for $S$, gives $$\operatorname{Lie}(C_G(S))=\mathfrak g^S=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\beta\in\Phi\cap\mathbf Q\alpha}\mathfrak g_\beta.$$ In particular this space contains the nonzero summand $\mathfrak g_\alpha$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(a), printed pp.428--429; Proposition 10.34; Chapter 12 character description of subtori.

proof.text: Put $H=C_G(S)$. Torus-centralizer reductivity makes $H$ reductive, and $T$ is still maximal in $H$ because a larger torus would be a larger torus in $G$. Among the smooth connected solvable normal subgroups of $H$, choose $R$ of maximal dimension, using the dimension bounds in the product lemma. If $N$ is any other such subgroup, its product $RN$ has these same properties and contains $R$; strict inclusion would increase dimension, so $RN=R$ and $N\subseteq R$. Thus $R$ is the radical. The perfect-field solvable-group theorem gives a smooth connected unipotent subgroup $R_u\triangleleft H$ and torus quotient $R/R_u$; normality in $H$, not just in $R$, is part of that theorem. Reductivity of $H$ makes $R_u=1$, hence $R$ is a torus. Connected-action rigidity applied to conjugation of $H$ on $R$ makes $R$ central. Since $S$ is itself central and a torus, $S\subseteq R$.

source.place: The proof of Corollary 17.62(b), printed p.372; maximal-dimension radical construction in Sections 6.44--6.46; used in Theorem 21.11(a).

proof.text: Apply the semisimple-rank formula to the reductive group $H$, its still-maximal torus $T$, and the central radical $R$ just constructed. It gives $R\subseteq T$ and $\operatorname{rank}(H/R)=\dim T-\dim R$. Since $S\subseteq R$ has codimension one in $T$, this rank is at most one. If it were zero, the included tori $R\subseteq T$ of equal dimension would be equal (their character kernel is saturated of rank zero). Then $T$ would be central in $H$, so $H\subseteq C_G(T)=T$. This contradicts the nonzero root summand in step 3. Thus $H=G_\alpha$ has semisimple rank one.

Apply the explicit rank-one classification to $(H,T)$. The extra $\mathbf G_m^r$ factor is central and contributes only zero weights. In the SL2 model put $\chi(\operatorname{diag}(z,z^{-1}))=z$; conjugation on the off-diagonal matrix units has characters $\pm2\chi$. For PGL2 the scalar quotient is the determinant-nonzero open of projective matrix space: on a chart where one entry is nonzero, scale that entry to $1$; the resulting affine charts glue by rescaling. This also gives matrix representatives for its $F$-points. In the PGL2 model put $\chi([\operatorname{diag}(a,b)])=a/b$; its tangent space is $\mathfrak{gl}_2/FI$, and the two off-diagonal classes have weights $\pm\chi$. In the GL2 model put $e_i(\operatorname{diag}(a,b))=a,b$; the off-diagonal weights are $\pm(e_1-e_2)$. Each listed weight space is one-dimensional and the remaining diagonal directions have weight zero, including in characteristic two. Comparing with step 3 shows that $\Phi\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ and $\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=1$. Choose the model or its conjugate by the off-diagonal matrix so that $\alpha$ is the positive weight just listed.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(b), printed p.429; Theorem 20.33; Examples 21.3--21.5 and 20.37.

proof.text: In these three models define $v:\operatorname{SL}_2\to H$ by $g\mapsto(1,g)$, $g\mapsto(1,[g])$, or $g\mapsto(1,g)$, respectively, and transport through the chosen pair isomorphism. The kernels are respectively trivial, $\mu_2$, and trivial; $\mu_2$ consists of scalar matrices $zI$ with $z^2=1$, so the kernel is central even in characteristic two. For the PGL2 map, an invertible matrix $g$ becomes determinant one after adjoining a root $c$ of $c^2=(\det g)^{-1}$ and replacing $g$ by $cg$; this is a faithfully flat rank-two extension, even in characteristic two. Their scheme-theoretic images are the derived subgroups specified by the classification. The map on upper unitriangular matrices is an isomorphism onto their image: in PGL2 a scalar matrix that is unitriangular is the identity, and the coordinate on this affine chart is the upper-right entry. Conjugating by a diagonal matrix multiplies this entry by the positive weight of step 6. The image is consequently a one-dimensional root subgroup with tangent space $\mathfrak g_\alpha$. Finally $v(\operatorname{diag}(z,z^{-1}))$ belongs to $T$, giving the asserted cocharacter.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(b), printed p.429; Proposition 20.32 and explicit models of Theorem 20.33.

proof.text: For the standard diagonal torus in each matrix model, a normalizing matrix must permute the two coordinate lines: these are its two distinct torus eigenspaces in the natural two-dimensional representation. Thus the normalizer consists of diagonal and antidiagonal matrices. For PGL2 use a GL2 representative over the algebraically closed field; normalizing the image torus implies normalizing its full inverse image, the diagonal torus in GL2. The same conclusion follows. The central product factor changes neither quotient. Hence $N_H(T)(F)/T(F)$ has exactly two elements, with nonidentity element represented by $v(w)$ for $w=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Its inclusion in $N_G(T)(F)/T(F)$ is injective, since both quotients have the same denominator $T(F)$. Call its image $s_\alpha$.

source.place: Theorem 21.11(d), printed pp.429--430; 20.39; standard normalizer matrices for GL2 and PGL2.

proof.text: The element $w$ inverts the SL2 diagonal coordinate and swaps the two GL2 diagonal entries. In the SL2 case $\alpha=2\chi$ and $\alpha^\vee:z\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(z,z^{-1})$, so $\langle\chi,\alpha^\vee\rangle=1$ and $s_\alpha\chi=-\chi=\chi-\alpha$. In the PGL2 case $\alpha=\chi$ and $\chi(\alpha^\vee(z))=z^2$, so $s_\alpha\chi=-\chi=\chi-2\alpha$. In the GL2 case $\alpha=e_1-e_2$, the pairings of $e_1,e_2$ with $\alpha^\vee$ are $1,-1$, and swapping them is precisely $x\mapsto x-\langle x,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha$. The central-factor characters are fixed and have pairing zero. Checking this integral basis proves the reflection identity for every $x\in X$ and gives $\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2$ in all three cases.

It therefore takes the unique nonidentity local normalizer class to the corresponding class there: $ns_\alpha n^{-1}=s_{n\alpha}$. Conjugating the reflection identity and using pairing preservation yields $s_{n\alpha}(x)=x-\langle x,n\alpha^\veeangle(n\alpha)$. Uniqueness now gives $n\alpha^\vee=(n\alpha)^\vee$. All weight and pairing computations were in free integer character lattices; none used differentials of characters.

reviewed.note: mechanical checks by tools/merge_delivery.py; mathematics reviewed in full by NT-cc-Q69-604939fb6 (reviewer sub-agent of L); spot-checked: I read the item, all four new nodes and every cited statement in full, and checked them against Milne iAG2017: 21.11(a)-(f) pp.428-430, 20.33/20.34 pp.418-419, 21.15, 17.59 p.371, 13.10-13.11 p.257. Steps 1-10 hold under the hypotheses in force. Step 1: weight decomposition plus Lie(C_G(T))=g^T, then self-centralizer. Step 2: the normalizer-components node makes W finite; the action, pairing invariance and Ad(n)g_a=g_{na} check by hand. Step 3: T_a=ker a for a primitive (also when p|m). Steps 4-5: radical via product lemma, perfect-solvable and rigidity, so R is a central torus containing S; the rank formula gives rank 1 and rank 0 contradicts C_G(T)=T. This is Milne's (a). Steps 6-9: weights, kernels, U+ isomorphism, normalizer and reflection formula verified in the SL2/PGL2/GL2 models, including characteristic 2 (Lie PGL2=gl2/F). Step 10: uniqueness from torsion-free X and perfect pairing; equivariance by conjugating T_a, G_a and s_a. New nodes: torus-fixed-subgroup (Milne 17.59), torus-normalizer-components (12.40, 13.10), semisimple-rank-formula (17.20) and split-rank-one-classification (20.33 with the errata rank-1 hypothesis). All four are true; I checked the classification independently on root data (the image of <.,a^v> is 2Z or Z, and the parity of k0 separates SL2 from GL2). The corrected derived groups SL2/PGL2/SL2 are right; Milne's text has a typo there. No new node is a duplicate after a dag-wide search, and none restates a clause of the item. The DAG stays acyclic, proof_deps equals the union of uses, every citation stays in unit sk-thm-sf-ctf-stability, and there is no SGA.
